summary: Sandipan Bhaumik draws on two years of customer work at Databricks and prior AWS experience to present a five-pillar framework for deploying AI agents at enterprise scale. He identifies a model-first anti-pattern where organizations rush to choose models, build controlled demos, then fail in production due to three gaps: observability, evaluation, and governance. The evaluation pillar requires numerical success metrics, golden data sets from domain experts, and a three-layer architecture: deterministic (formats, NER, PII), semantic (LLM-as-judge for groundedness), and behavioral (tool-call correctness, duplicate API detection). The observability pillar is illustrated with a retail banking chatbot handling an overdraft-fee waiver request—tracing reveals intent classification, customer database lookups, RAG-based policy retrieval, reasoning, and guardrail checks. Without traces, customer disputes become unresolvable and regulators block production deployment. Online monitoring on traces enables real-time fallback strategies. The data foundation pillar consumes 60% of project time because agents do not forgive bad data. Data splits into question data and tracking data, each needing dedicated strategy. Databricks provides Delta Lake, Unity Catalog, Mosaic AI, Genie, and Agent Bricks with MLflow. Multi-agent orchestration introduces three patterns: orchestrator-worker, choreography, and human-in-the-loop. Governance covers audit trails, pre-validation PII detection (47 breaches caught in testing), prompt versioning, and model change management. The retail banking case study demonstrates the full framework: an £85K failed POC was replaced by an eight-week engagement where model selection came in week seven, preceded by evaluation data collection (200 cases from human agents), success metrics (60% deflection, 85% accuracy), automated evaluation pipeline, and data foundation setup. Six weeks post-launch, stale policy documents that were not re-embedded caused CSAT drops caught by tracing. Bhaumik introduces a production incident playbook: detect (eval dashboard), diagnose (tracing), contain (prompt versioning, fault tolerance patterns including saga, compensation, circuit breaker, human deflection), fix (test case library), and ITSM integration. Three governance lessons address test case library ownership, meaningful prompt commit messages, and behavioral eval cost control via subset testing in CI. He closes by sharing a QR code to his LinkedIn profile and a free weekly newsletter where he shares field learnings from customer engagements, along with downloadable artifacts including evaluation checklists and tracing setup guides.

sections.title: Speaker Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Sandipan Bhaumik introduces himself as technical lead for data and AI at Databricks, previously principal architect at AWS for five years. He frames the session as a playbook drawn from two years of customer work across B2B software and regulated financial services.

sections.title: The Model-First Anti-Pattern
sections.summary: Bhaumik describes the recurring pattern: organizations under leadership pressure start by debating which model to use, build features in controlled environments, impress leadership with demos, then fail in production with unpredictable behavior, no ROI, and wasted effort.

sections.title: Three Gaps and Five Pillars Framework
sections.summary: Three insights from failed engagements—observability gap, evaluation gap, governance gap—led to a five-pillar framework: evaluation, observability, data foundation, orchestration, and governance. Each pillar is introduced including the split of data foundation into question data and tracking data, and the exponential complexity of multi-agent orchestration.

sections.title: Evaluation Pillar: Metrics, Golden Data Sets, and Three Layers
sections.summary: Deep dive into evaluation as specification for AI systems. Success must be defined numerically with business-relevant metrics like deflection rates and acceptable false positives. Golden data sets should be built from domain expert answers including edge cases, with automated testing pipelines. Three architectural layers: deterministic (formats, regex, classic ML for NER and PII), non-deterministic semantic (LLM-as-a-judge for groundedness and safety), and behavioral (tool-call correctness, loops, duplicate API calls). The behavioral layer is illustrated with an account-balance query where the agent made three database calls instead of one—harmless in demos but costly at production scale.

sections.title: Observability Pillar: Tracing, Banking Chatbot Example, and Online Monitoring
sections.summary: Bhaumik explains observability through a retail banking chatbot handling an overdraft-fee waiver dispute. Traces reveal intent classification (with confidence scores and timing), customer database API calls, RAG-based policy document retrieval, reasoning steps, and final guardrail checks. Without this trace visualization, customer disputes are unresolvable. European regulators mandate tracing before production deployment. Online monitoring on traces enables real-time detection of duplicate API calls and failing calls, with fallback strategies such as retry limits before escalating to humans.

sections.title: Data Foundation Pillar: Question Data, Tracking Data, and Databricks Stack
sections.summary: Bhaumik identifies data foundation as the most important pillar, consuming 60% of project time. Unlike humans, agents do not forgive bad data—they return wrong answers confidently. Data splits into question data (serving AI outcomes) and tracking data (observability traces). The Databricks stack supports this: cloud storage, Delta Lake, Unity Catalog for centralized permissions and PII tagging, Mosaic AI, Genie for text-to-SQL on tracing data, and Agent Bricks with MLflow for LLM-as-judges. A centralized tracing layer collects data across frameworks like CrewAI and LangChain.

sections.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration Patterns
sections.summary: Bhaumik presents three orchestration patterns: orchestrator-worker (central control, specialized agents), choreography (autonomous agents on a message bus, parallel execution, lower latency), and human-in-the-loop (escalation on confidence threshold breaches). He references his deep-dive YouTube video covering state management, fault tolerance, and enterprise scaling.

sections.title: Governance Pillar: Audit Trails, PII, Prompt and Model Change Management
sections.summary: Governance covers regulatory audit trails, pre-validation PII detection using NER (47 breaches caught in testing), prompt versioning as enterprise change management, and model change management requiring evaluation against enterprise-specific data sets. The talk transitions toward Databricks Agent Bricks as the productized embodiment of all five pillars.

sections.title: Retail Banking Case Study: From Failed POC to Production Success
sections.summary: Bhaumik details a retail banking case study. The bank received 20,000 calls/month with 60% being simple queries suitable for deflection. A prior £85K six-month POC failed with no one able to explain why. His team's eight-week engagement spent weeks 1-2 building the evaluation layer (200 cases from human agents, success metrics defined: 60% deflection, 85% accuracy, automated evaluation pipeline). Weeks 3-6 focused on data foundation: API connections, tracing infrastructure, distributed storage, catching duplicate API calls. Model selection happened in week 7—quick because the evaluation data set enabled direct comparison. The evaluation data set is a living system that grows over time. Six weeks post-launch, the bank changed interest rate policies but failed to re-embed new documents; the tracing system detected stale answers causing CSAT drops, enabling rapid diagnosis and fix.

sections.title: Production Incident Playbook
sections.summary: Bhaumik introduces a production incident playbook connecting all five pillars. The flow: detect using eval dashboard, diagnose using tracing, contain (version prompts, remove problematic prompts, deflect to humans, apply fault tolerance patterns including saga, compensation, and circuit breaker), fix using test case library and LLM-as-judge reports, then add new test cases to the living evaluation data set. The playbook must integrate with existing ITSM systems for alerting the right person at the right time.

sections.title: Three Governance Lessons and Takeaway Artifacts
sections.summary: Three lessons: (1) Test case libraries need governance—an owner and categorization (e.g., security, login) so failures map to test categories. (2) Prompt versioning via Git requires governance on commit messages documenting the failure addressed and what the change corrects, not simple commits. (3) Behavioral evals are expensive at scale; manage cost by running subset tests in CI and full tests only on merge to main branch. Bhaumik shares a QR code linking to downloadable artifacts: evaluation checklists, tracing setup guides with open source technologies, and example templates.

sections.title: Closing: LinkedIn and Newsletter
sections.summary: Bhaumik shares a QR code linking to his LinkedIn profile and mentions a free weekly newsletter where he shares field learnings from working with customers on AI production topics. He thanks the audience to applause.
